title: Greenhouse API: Which of the 5 APIs to Use (2026)
summary: Greenhouse API lets you connect systems to recruiting data via HTTP. Set your authentication credentials, account for rate limits, and handle API errors.
body_markdown:
## A minimal working Greenhouse API request, with pagination


Start with one authenticated GET against the Harvest API's candidates endpoint, and you have a working first request. A correct pagination loop follows the Link header the server returns instead of counting pages yourself.


The key you just put in a secrets manager is what makes the first call possible, so read it from there at run time.


### Making your first Greenhouse Harvest API request


Harvest uses HTTP Basic authentication: the API key is the username and the password is left blank. Export the key from your secrets manager into an environment variable, then call the candidates endpoint with a small page size.


```text
curl -u "$GREENHOUSE_HARVEST_KEY:" \
"https://harvest.greenhouse.io/v1/candidates?per_page=10"
```


The trailing colon after the key matters. Without it, curl prompts for a password and a scheduled job hangs with nobody watching. Whoever owns the key owns this failure, so name them in the job's runbook.


### Reading the Greenhouse API response


When the call succeeds, you get a JSON array of candidate objects, each with its own id, name fields, and nested records such as applications. An empty array means you've run past the end or your filters match nothing.


You will see an authentication failure as a 401 status, which almost always means a wrong key or a missing colon.


A 403 means the key is valid but lacks permission for that endpoint, and whoever administers the key's permissions has to fix that; retrying will not.


Check the response headers too, because that's where the pagination instructions live.


### Paging through all Greenhouse API results


To page through everything, use the Link header, which carries rel values such as next and last; the documented loop follows it.


Request the first page with per_page, read the next URL from the header, request that URL exactly as given, and stop when the header has no next link.


Don't rebuild the URL yourself or increment a page number: the server's link is the contract, and hand-built URLs drift when parameters change.


If a run dies partway, you want it to resume rather than re-pull everything or silently skip records. Persist the last URL you completed.


Activepieces lets you skip writing that loop by hand: describe the Greenhouse sync in its built-in chat and it publishes a live flow in your account, the same artifact a builder would have assembled step by step.


The run trace for each execution records what every step received, so the last page requested and the status it returned are on the record rather than inferred.
